sections.history: Tirumullaivoyil lies today at the northern edge of Chennai, between Ambattur and Avadi, in what was once Thondai Nadu, the old Tamil country around Kanchipuram. It is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams, honoured in the Tevaram hymns of the saint Sundarar. The name means the gateway of the jasmine, and the word Vada, northern, sets it apart from Then Tirumullaivoyil, its southern namesake near Sirkazhi. Tradition credits the Cholas with raising the present stone temple in the ninth century, and inscriptions of the tenth century, including the time of Parthivendravarman, a feudatory of Uttama Chola, are reported at the site. For centuries a village shrine, the temple is now the spiritual anchor of a fast-growing suburb.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered through a gateway tower on its northern side, while the sanctum of Masilamaniswarar itself faces east. Built in the Dravidian manner, it carries the sober, well-proportioned character of Chola stonework in its sculpture and inscribed walls. The Lord is worshipped as a linga, and the goddess Kodiyidai Nayaki, also known as Piraisoodi Amman, has her own shrine. A much-remarked detail is the Nandi, which is said not to face the Lord but to look the other way, recalling the bull sent to accompany the king into battle. A carving on the temple wall is said to show the king cutting through the jasmine creeper to uncover the linga.
sections.legends: The temple's story begins with a king. Thondaiman, ruler of the Thondai country, marched out to subdue two Kurumbar chieftains, Vaanan and Onan, who held the forests to the north; some tellings name a third, Kanthan. On the way his elephant became entangled in a dense thicket of jasmine, mullai. The king cut the creeper free with his sword, and a linga hidden beneath it was found to be bleeding. Horrified, he turned his blade upon himself, but Shiva and Parvati appeared, stayed his hand and bade him raise a temple on the spot. The Lord also sent Nandi to go with him, and the campaign was won. The linga bled yet bore no stain of fault, and so the Lord is called Masilamani, the flawless gem. The goddess is Kodiyidai Nayaki, she whose waist is slender as a creeper, a reminder of the jasmine vine that once hid the Lord.
sections.festivals: The calendar here turns mostly on the monthly rhythm of worship: Pradosham, Amavasya, Pournami and Kiruthigai days bring devotees in numbers, with special worship offered to Nandi. A Chithirai festival is held in April or May, and Maha Shivaratri is observed through the night as at every Shiva temple. The festival days follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm dates locally before you plan a visit.
sections.experience: Come in the quiet of the early morning, before the road outside fills. Many visitors begin at the Nandi, whose averted gaze tells the story of the king, and then go in to the sanctum of Masilamaniswarar. The temple is especially loved by those praying for marriage: unmarried devotees are traditionally said to offer archana to Nandi and to circle the shrine twenty-seven times. Take a moment in the goddess's shrine, where the slender creeper of her name keeps the memory of the jasmine alive. Though the suburb has grown thick around it, the temple retains the calm of an old village sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning until around midday and again from late afternoon until about eight in the evening; published timings differ, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is at Thirumullaivoyal on the Chennai–Avadi road, between Ambattur and Avadi in north-western Chennai. Tirumullaivayil railway station on the suburban line is about 1.5 km away, and Ambattur is about 2 km. City buses run along the Avadi road, and autorickshaws and cabs are easily found.
